Threat.value: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger
Unusual silence makes me feel something dangerous is about to happen
I notice potential weapons or dangerous objects in any environment

Memory.value: When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred.
When I remember the event I feel overwhelming grief
I remember the frightening event as a few moments, and each moment is a picture in my mind.

Negative Appraisals.value: My reactions since the event mean that I am going crazy
I can't stop bad things from happening to me

issues.item: Failed to Protect: I should have protected others and I failed
issues.explanation: For an 18-year-old whose index trauma is witnessing domestic violence in childhood, this appraisal is hard to reconcile with the likely role in the trauma. A child witness may feel guilty, but 'I should have protected others' implies a level of responsibility and agency that is clinically implausible enough to question for this trauma context. The rest of the profile coheres around fear, helplessness, fragmented sensory memory, and hypervigilant threat monitoring; this single appraisal stands out as inconsistent with the demographics/trauma role.

vignette: At ten years old, Malik learned to read a room by the sharp intake of breath before a door slammed. He had been sitting cross-legged on the kitchen linoleum, tracing the grout lines, when the shouting began. What seared into him was not a linear story but a series of frozen frames: his father’s fist tightening, the heavy oak chair lifting an inch off the floor, the way his mother’s silence suddenly turned brittle and loud. When a plate shattered near his feet, Malik’s body locked exactly where he had been sitting, knees drawn up, shoulders hunched forward. He did not move until the footsteps receded. Those frames never faded. Years later, they returned not as narratives but as sudden, weightless snapshots that hijacked his breathing. The grief that followed was immediate and crushing, a heavy tide that left him unable to speak or function for hours. Separately, his body would sometimes settle into the exact posture of a boy waiting for the next blow, knees drawn up, shoulders hunched forward, holding the position long after the moment had passed. He navigated his days by controlling his environment. He avoided unfamiliar parking structures and back alleys, convinced that stepping into unfamiliar spaces meant he could not assess the danger. He treated sudden quiet not as peace, but as a held breath, certain that unusual silence meant something dangerous was about to happen. In crowds, he tracked movement like a radar, his eyes snapping to belt holsters, loose tools, anything that could become a weapon. When a stranger or even a familiar voice reached out without warning, his stomach dropped into a cold knot of pure discomfort, his muscles bracing before he even registered who had touched him. At eighteen, he joined the police academy, chasing control in a uniform that promised authority. But the badge only magnified what he feared. During his first solo patrol, a community member rushed forward to grab his sleeve, and the unexpected contact sent a jolt through him so violent he nearly stepped back, his hand instinctively flying to his hip. He diverted from the assigned route, opting to circle back through familiar streets where every alley and storefront felt documented. He watched other rookies laugh during quiet stretches in the cruiser, but he sat in the stillness with his pulse hammering. He began to distrust his own responses. When he hesitated during a routine traffic stop because a driver’s hand lingered near the door handle, he told himself he was losing his mind. He carried a quiet conviction that he could not stop bad things from happening to him. Beside it sat the fear that his own reactions meant he was going crazy. He simply could not rely on himself to navigate the threshold between a normal day and a catastrophe. He came to the clinic on a Tuesday, the weight of his uniform feeling heavier than standard issue. During a community outreach event, a child had run up and tapped his shoulder to show him a drawing. Malik flinched so hard he dropped his clipboard, and the sudden, unbidden wave of grief and bodily tension left him standing frozen in the parking lot while civilians stared. He went home and stared at his service weapon, not with pride, but with the terrifying certainty that his reactions meant he was broken beyond repair. He scheduled an intake, terrified that he would never trust his own instincts again, yet hoping that somewhere, someone could teach him how to stand in a room without bracing for the door to break.
